items.title: Why every kilogram matters

predictQuestion.question: Your lander is 500 kg over what the rocket can carry. What happens?
options: The rocket burns a little longer and makes up for it
It cannot reach the destination: something must come off
It arrives, just a few hours late

steps: A rocket can only push a fixed mass to the Moon or Mars. That number is its capacity.
Most of a rocket is fuel. Adding payload means needing even more fuel to lift that fuel.
So past the limit there is no 'a bit late': the mission simply does not fit.
Planners keep a margin of roughly 10–20% for growth, because designs always get heavier.
items.applyTemplate: Your design weighs {totalMassKg} kg against the {rocketName}'s {capacityKg} kg: a margin of {marginPct}.

items.title: Bigger rockets, bigger bills

predictQuestion.question: Switching to a heavier rocket gives you more capacity. What is the catch?
options: There is none, bigger is always better
It costs more, leaving less budget for parts and crew
It is always less reliable

steps: A heavier rocket lifts more mass, so you can carry more supplies and spares.
It also costs far more per launch, and that comes out of the same budget as everything else.
Each rocket has its own track record. Reliability is the share of launches that work.
Good planners pick the smallest rocket that still leaves a healthy mass margin.
items.applyTemplate: The {rocketName} costs ${rocketCostM}M of your ${budgetM}M budget, carries {capacityKg} kg and is about {reliabilityPct} reliable.

items.title: Surviving the dark

predictQuestion.question: Your base runs on solar panels. What keeps the heaters and air system running at night?
options: The panels still work a little in starlight
Batteries charged during the day, or a power source that ignores the Sun
Nothing: the crew sleeps until sunrise

steps: Solar panels only produce power while the Sun is up.
Life support never switches off, so night-time power must be stored in batteries.
The battery has to hold the base's load for every hour of darkness, with some to spare.
Long nights, like the lunar night, need huge batteries, so some bases add a fission power unit.
items.applyTemplate: Your base needs about {nightNeedWh} Wh to get through {darkHours} dark hours; your batteries hold {batteryWh} Wh.

items.title: What a person uses every day

predictQuestion.question: Roughly how much oxygen does one astronaut breathe per day?
options: About 80 grams
About 0.8 kg
About 8 kg

steps: Each crew member uses roughly 0.8 kg of oxygen, 2 kg of food and 3 kg of water a day (approximate).
Multiply by the crew and the days, and supplies quickly become the heaviest thing on board.
Recyclers win back most of the water and some oxygen, so less has to be launched.
Running out of any one of the three ends the mission, so planners add reserve days.
items.applyTemplate: Your crew of {crewCount} uses about {oxygenPerDay} kg oxygen and {waterPerDay} kg water a day; with your recyclers the supplies last {supplyDays} days.

items.title: Science only counts if it gets home

predictQuestion.question: Your instruments collect 10 GB a day, but your radio can send only 4 GB. What happens to the rest?
options: It is sent later, for free
It piles up on board and may never reach scientists
The instruments slow down automatically

steps: Data only becomes science once it reaches Earth.
How much you can send is the radio's data rate times the hours you are in contact each day.
Anything you collect beyond that waits in storage, and storage fills up.
Better antennas or more contact time are often worth more than another instrument.
items.applyTemplate: You collect {dataGenGbPerDay} GB/day and can send {dataReturnGbPerDay} GB/day in {contactHours} contact hours: {dataReturnPct} gets home.

items.title: Go, no-go: how a launch is called

predictQuestion.question: Before launch, the flight director asks every console 'go or no-go'. Why ask everyone?
options: Tradition, the answer is always go
Each console knows one system best, and one real problem can stop the launch
To decide the launch time by vote

steps: Each controller watches one system: power, life support, communications, the rocket.
In the poll, each one says go or no-go for their own system, out loud.
One no-go holds the launch until the problem is understood and fixed.
Known small risks can be accepted, but only if everyone hears them first.
items.applyTemplate: Your checklist right now: {okCount} ok, {warnCount} warnings and {failCount} failing checks.

items.title: Dust on the panels

predictQuestion.question: A dust storm leaves a thin layer on your solar panels. What changes?
options: Nothing, dust is see-through
Less sunlight reaches the cells, so less power
The panels overheat and make more power

steps: Fine dust settles on panels and blocks part of the sunlight.
Power drops with every layer; storms also darken the sky itself.
Mars rovers have lost much of their power this way, and some were saved when wind cleaned them.
Bases plan extra panel area, cleaning, or power that does not need sunlight.
items.applyTemplate: Your panels are rated {solarRatedW} W; dust has cut them by about {dustNowPct} so far.

items.title: Talking to Mars takes minutes

predictQuestion.question: Mission Control spots an alarm on your Mars base. How soon can their answer reach you?
options: Instantly
A few seconds
Several minutes to over 20 minutes

steps: Radio travels at the speed of light, but Mars is tens to hundreds of millions of km away.
A one-way message takes roughly 4 to 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are (approximate).
So for urgent problems the crew cannot wait for Earth's answer.
That is why you set standing orders: rules the crew follows on their own.
items.applyTemplate: Today the one-way delay to {destinationName} is about {delayMin} min, so urgent events are handled under your standing orders.
